Below is a concise, evidence-based overview of “cell line organoids” (organoid systems initiated with or modeled after established immortalized or transformed cell lines), how they are made, their advantages and limits, and key application domains.

What “cell line organoids” are and where they fit
- Organoids are 3D cultures that better preserve tissue architecture, cell-type composition, and (epi)genetic heterogeneity than traditional 2D immortalized cell lines, yet they are more complex than simple spheroids and still face standardization and throughput challenges relative to cell lines and high-throughput cell-line banks <cite id="bf13eb6b-0">Organoids retain the 3D structure of the original tissues, faithfully summarizing the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity of the original tissue</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Two-dimensional immortalized cell lines are generally considered non-physiological due to lack of tissue architecture and genetic drift across batches</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-3">Organoids can reproduce tissue layers and structures and can be frozen like cell lines, offering more realistic in vitro modeling than cell lines</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-4">Organoid technology accelerates disease modeling but requires standardization and scaled production; throughput is limited by ECM gels and automation</cite>. 
- In the central nervous system, “spheroids” can be formed from primary cells or immortalized lines, whereas “organoids” are typically stem-cell–derived 3D self-organizing structures; both leverage 3D cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions to approximate in vivo organization for drug screening, developmental biology, and pathology <cite id="7e8f2221-0">Spheroids are 3D aggregates from primary cells or immortalized cell lines; organoids are stem-cell–derived 3D aggregates that self-organize to recapitulate tissue characteristics</cite>. 
- Conceptually, organoids are positioned between conventional cell lines and patient-derived xenografts (PDX), aiming to combine genetic fidelity and physiological complexity with practicality for screening and precision medicine <cite id="bf13eb6b-0">Organoids fill the gap between cell line and PDX, support existing model systems, and extend research to the human context</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Organoids are derived from small patient samples with high efficiency and better recapitulate architecture and functions than cell lines</cite>.

How cell line–based organoids are generated
- Epithelial/intestinal organoids (gut and pancreas): Canonical protocols culture Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells in Matrigel with niche factors (WNT agonists via R-spondin, EGF, Noggin) to sustain self-renewal and crypt–villus morphogenesis; similar strategies adapted human intestinal and colon organoids and informed later organoid engineering <cite id="335bd1d1-0">Single Lgr5+ stem cells embedded in Matrigel with WNT, Noggin, R-spondin and EGF form continuously expanding crypt–villus organoids with near-physiological epithelium</cite><cite id="335bd1d1-2">Human intestinal organoids were adapted from the 2009 system; organoids from colon and stomach with Lgr5+ stem cells followed</cite><cite id="335bd1d1-3">Intestinal organoids derived from PSCs can be matured in Matrigel into polarized epithelium with villus-like and crypt-like structures</cite><cite id="335bd1d1-4">A cytokine- and Matrigel-free protocol was developed to enable higher-throughput intestinal organoid screening</cite>. 
- Patient-derived and hybrid models: When primary tissue is scarce or difficult, organoids can be initiated from tumor biopsies and then expanded or complemented with PDX to generate organoid biobanks; PDX-organoid hybrids reduce time/cost while providing sufficient material for downstream organoid establishment <cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Organoids can be derived from small patient samples with high efficiency and are suitable for drug response prediction</cite><cite id="ae19e242-4">A PDX-organoid model takes less time and cost than PDX and provides adequate tissue for organoid establishment</cite>. 
- Prostate cancer organoids from established cell lines: To address representativeness limits of traditional PCa cell lines, organoids were directly generated “from currently available cell lines,” reproducing recurrent copy-number and mutation profiles (e.g., PTEN loss, CHD1, SPOP, FOXA1), with high intra-organoid genetic consistency and stability over time; subsequent protocols for biopsy-derived PCa organoids established long-term cultures spanning luminal/basal lineages and aggressive disease states <cite id="ae19e242-0">Gao et al. developed seven metastatic PCa organoids using available cell lines that reproduced PTEN loss and CHD1, SPOP, and FOXA1 alterations and remained genetically stable; Jarno et al. established a biopsy-derived culture protocol supporting luminal/basal lineages and advanced cancers</cite><cite id="ae19e242-1">PCa organoids from cell lines retained mutation profiles including PTEN loss and CHD1, SPOP, FOXA1 mutations and showed genetic stability over time</cite>. 
- Practical prostate organoid culture from tissue and lines: Organoids can be initiated from diverse PCa specimens and grown in Matrigel with optimized media; growth rates are slower than many other cancers; protocols address overgrowth by benign epithelium and basal cells, yielding luminal phenotypes; additionally, PCa cell lines (e.g., LNCaP, C4-2B) and single luminal progenitors can generate prostate organoids with androgen-dependent or non-androgen-dependent characteristics <cite id="ae19e242-3">Prostate organoids embedded in Matrigel using optimized media maintain acinar/solid structures and show slower growth than other tumor organoids; protocols reduce basal cell presence to yield luminal phenotypes</cite><cite id="ae19e242-0">LNCaP and C4-2B can produce prostate organoids with androgen-dependent and non-androgen-dependent models, respectively</cite><cite id="ae19e242-4">Organoids from mouse and human tissues recapitulate AR signaling, basal/luminal markers, and fusion/alteration phenotypes; LNCaP, C4-2B, and single luminal progenitors can produce PCa organoids</cite>. 
- Neural organoids and spheroids from immortalized lines: Brain organoids/“mini-brains” are commonly derived from pluripotent stem cells via self-organization protocols (e.g., SFEBq, dual-SMAD inhibition spheroid culture) to recapitulate regional development and enable disease modeling; in parallel, 3D brain spheroids routinely use primary cells or immortalized lines as the starting material, and organoids can be scaled with bioreactors and vascularization strategies to mitigate diffusion limits <cite id="7e8f2221-2">Neural organoids generated from pluripotent stem cells via SFEBq or neural spheroid protocols differentiate into region-specific 3D neural tissues</cite><cite id="7e8f2221-0">Spheroids are 3D aggregates from primary cells or immortalized lines, whereas organoids self-organize from stem cells to recapitulate tissue characteristics</cite><cite id="7e8f2221-3">Brain organoids derived from iPSCs are cultured in Matrigel droplets, often in bioreactors; vascularization strategies with vascular spheroids or ETV2 overexpression address diffusion limits</cite>.

Advantages and key applications of cell line–based organoids
- Genetic tractability and fidelity: Prostate cancer organoids derived from established cell lines closely reproduce hallmark alterations (e.g., PTEN loss, ERG–TMPRSS2 fusions, SPOP/FOXA1), offering models where genotype-to-phenotype relationships can be interrogated and tracked over time <cite id="ae19e242-0">Cell line–derived PCa organoids reproduced recurrent alterations (PTEN loss, CHD1, SPOP, FOXA1) and remained genetically stable</cite>. 
- Disease modeling and drug discovery: Organoids support precision oncology by retaining tumor heterogeneity and drug response features; prostate organoid biobanks have been established to probe oncogenic pathways (e.g., SPOP mutation effects on AR binding) and to test therapeutics in patient-specific matrices <cite id="ae19e242-2">Prostate organoids retained TME complexity and AR-related molecular programs; SPOP mutations altered AR binding patterns mirroring primary tumors</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Organoids better recapitulate architecture and functions for disease modeling and drug response prediction</cite>. 
- Virus and infection modeling: Organoids mimic organ-level physiology better than 2D lines, enabling realistic infection and antiviral screening while remaining amenable to genetic manipulation; however, cost and scalability constraints still limit full replacement of cell-line and animal models <cite id="bf13eb6b-3">Organoids can reproduce tissue layers and structures, can be frozen like cell lines, and better simulate in vivo phenomena for complex disease modeling</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-4">Organoid technology reduces animal use but needs standardization and scaled production; current culture costs and handling limit large-scale replacement</cite>. 
- Neurodevelopmental and neurological disease: Neural organoids capture early cortical development gene expression and cytoarchitecture, enabling mechanistic studies and drug testing; spheroids initiated from immortalized lines provide a practical entry point when primary tissue is limited <cite id="7e8f2221-3">Brain organoids recapitulate fetal neocortex gene programs and support diverse readouts for drug screening and mechanistic studies</cite><cite id="7e8f2221-0">Spheroids from immortalized lines are widely used as precursors to organoid systems</cite>. 
- High-throughput and engineering: For epithelial organoids, medium and matrix optimizations (e.g., cytokine-free, low-Matrigel conditions) enable compatibility with automated screening and microfluidic platforms, expanding throughput while retaining core biological features <cite id="335bd1d1-4">A cytokine- and Matrigel-free protocol was developed to support high-throughput screening of intestinal organoids</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Some groups culture organoids in lower ECM to adapt to high-throughput screening using microfluidic systems</cite>.

Limitations, caveats, and engineering strategies
- Representativeness and drift: Immortalized 2D lines often diverge from tissue-of-origin genotype and phenotypes and exhibit non-physiological architecture; cell line–derived organoids can close this gap but may still carry founder-effect biases and genetic drift over time <cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Cell lines established decades ago no longer faithfully represent their tissue of origin and show genetic drift across batches</cite><cite id="ae19e242-0">Prostate cell lines fail to reflect recurrent lesions like TMPRSS2-ERG fusions and CHD1 deletions, SPOP and FOXA1 mutations</cite>. 
- Organoid fidelity vs. throughput: While organoids better model physiology, ECM gels and complex architectures challenge automation and high-throughput screening; strategies include lower ECM density, microfluidics, and standardization of culture conditions to balance fidelity and scalability <cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Organoids’ ECM gels limit automated high-throughput handling; low-gel or gel-free conditions and microfluidics are being explored</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-4">Standardization and scalable production are necessary for broader applications</cite>. 
- Protocol and lineage control: Prostate organoid protocols must manage overgrowth by benign epithelium and basal cell populations to maintain luminal phenotypes; growth kinetics are slower in some cancers, requiring patient stratification and careful readouts <cite id="ae19e242-3">PC organoids initially face overgrowth by benign epithelium and basal cells; optimized cultures yield luminal phenotypes and show slower growth rates</cite>. 
- Genetic and phenotypic engineering: Combining organoid culture with CRISPR enables precise mutation modeling (e.g., AR pathway variants, SPOP alterations) and co-culture/biobank strategies to expand genetic diversity and functional readouts <cite id="bf13eb6b-0">CRISPR–Cas9 with organoids provides opportunities to study tumor gene mutations</cite><cite id="ae19e242-2">SPOP mutation impacts AR binding patterns in organoids, paralleling native tumors</cite>.

Practical takeaways and when to use cell line–based organoids
- Use established cell-line organoids when primary tissue is limited or when you need genetically defined, tractable models with known driver landscapes (e.g., CRPC/LNCaP/C4-2B prostate organoids) to study oncogenic programs, drug response, and pathway perturbations <cite id="ae19e242-0">Cell line–derived PCa organoids reproduce recurrent alterations and offer genetically stable systems for modeling</cite><cite id="ae19e242-4">LNCaP and C4-2B produce organoids with distinct androgen dependence, useful for precision models</cite>. 
- For infectious disease and multi-cellular organ-level mechanisms, spheroids initiated from immortalized lines and organoids from PSCs provide practical platforms before scaling up to patient-derived organoids; integrate bioreactor culture and vascularization to improve viability and maturation <cite id="7e8f2221-0">Spheroids from immortalized lines are established practices for brain models</cite><cite id="7e8f2221-3">Bioreactor culture and vascularization strategies (e.g., co-assembly with vascular spheroids or ETV2 activation) mitigate diffusion limits</cite>. 
- To maximize relevance and reproducibility, pair cell line–derived organoids with rigorous barcoding/longitudinal genotyping, matrix/medium standardization, and cross-checks against patient-derived organoids or PDX; where feasible, move to cytokine/matrix-optimized or microfluidic formats for higher-throughput screening <cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Longitudinal culture standardization and low-gel/microfluidic adaptations improve throughput and comparability</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-0">Organoid banks and CRISPR-based perturbations can build comprehensive experimental platforms</cite>.

Uncertainties and open needs
- Organ specificity: While strong evidence exists for gut and prostate systems, direct protocols for liver organoids initiated from widely used hepatocellular carcinoma lines (e.g., HepG2, Huh7) were not captured in the retrieved snippets; similar gaps exist for definitive “TOP-NHDF feeder” protocols for human gut organoids beyond foundational niche-factor culture. Additional targeted literature would clarify matrix and growth factor dependencies for liver and epithelial systems. 
- Definitions and reporting: The boundary between spheroids and organoids can be blurry; clearer reporting of starting cell sources (primary vs immortalized), self-organization cues, and co-culture composition would aid comparability across studies <cite id="7e8f2221-0">There is controversy over the boundary between spheroids and organoids, with organoids defined as self-organizing stem-cell–derived 3D aggregates</cite>. 
- Scale and cost: Despite engineering advances, cost and scalability constraints of ECM-based organoids remain; broader adoption will depend on standardized workflows and scalable platforms (e.g., fully defined media, decellularized matrices, perfusion/organ-on-chip) <cite id="bf13eb6b-3">Organoid culture is expensive and difficult to scale due to ECM substrates and handling challenges</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-4">Production at scale and standardization are fundamental needs for translational use</cite>.

In summary, “cell line organoids” leverage established immortalized lines to seed, engineer, or otherwise emulate organ-level physiology in 3D, offering genetic tractability and improved fidelity over 2D lines while retaining many practical advantages of cell-line systems. They are now central tools in cancer precision modeling (e.g., prostate), CNS development and disease, and infectious/virus studies, with active engineering to improve scalability and standardization <cite id="ae19e242-0">Cell line–derived PCa organoids reproduce recurrent mutations with stability and model disease mechanisms</cite><cite id="7e8f2221-2">Neural organoids self-organize into region-specific structures enabling human brain development and disease modeling</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-0">Organoids bridge cell lines and PDX and support drug screening, gene editing, and biobanking</cite>.

Title: Disease modeling in organoid cultures: a new tool for studying viruses
Snippet: Organoids are an experimental model similar to cell lines that have been used for decades to study cellular mechanisms and to develop novel treatments for various diseases. Although in vitro assay systems using cell lines have several advantages, they cannot directly mimic in vivo systems; instead, organoids could be used as alternatives to mimic the actual situation in organs. Organoid systems also have several advantages over cell lines, since there is no loss of function due to immortality, as is the case in vivo, and they are easy to manipulate and observe. Moreover, organoids can reproduce the cell layers and tissue structures that can be seen in organs. This suggests that organoids can be cultured for longer periods, frozen like cell lines, and used to study physiological phenomena more realistically than is possible with cell lines using next-generation in vitro analysis methods. 

The bio-similarity of organoids makes it easier to proceed with the sophisticated modeling of complex diseases, such as infectious diseases, genetic diseases, and cancer. The modeling of these diseases is not restricted to discovering new treatments for the diseases, but could also yield insights into the mechanism of disease onset. One of the advantages of organoid models over cell lines is their ability to reproduce complex interactions between organs, which could otherwise only be investigated in animal experiments, to evaluate the efficacy and toxicity of drugs. 

However, organoids are not yet reliable enough to completely replace experiments using cell lines or animal models. Organoid culture systems have developed rapidly since they were first introduced and are still developing, but organoid cultures are expensive and have difficulty replicating the scale of massive cell-line culture systems. The external substrates or scaffolds used for 3D culture are expensive and difficult to handle, which imposes a limitation on culture. In addition, imbalances in the distribution of nutrients, growth and differentiation factors, and the number of the stem cells obtained from the organ may occur during the culture, preventing the quantification of growing organoids. Moreover, one of the main obstacles in current organoid systems is that the histological structure and functions of organoids are still limited in comparison to actual organs. However, the most important aspect of organoids is that they are in vitro experimental models that can simulate in vivo phenomena, and due to this advantage, we believe that organoids will replace or support existing models as a higher-level experimental model.

Title: Urological cancer organoids, patients' avatars for precision medicine: past, present and future
Snippet: Over the past century, only seven prostate cancer cell lines have been established, six from biopsy samples of patients with metastatic prostate cancer and one from circulating tumour cells (CTCs). Although cell lines are easy to culture, they fail to reflect common recurrent genetic lesions in prostate cancer such as TMPRSS2-ERG and CHD1 deletions, SPOP and FOXA1 mutations [36]. 

To fix this research gap, Schroe et al. [37] firstly reported  [38]. However, prostate cancer xenotransplantation has a low success rate ranging from 20 to 75% in subcutaneous models [39]. Nonetheless, the emergence of organoids is a promising solution. 

In 2014, Gao et al. [40] first developed seven metastatic prostate cancer organoids (PCOs) using currently available cell lines and demonstrated that PCOs could reproduce characteristic copy number and mutation profiles commonly found in prostate cancer, including the loss of PTEN and CHD1, SPOP and FOXA1 mutations (Fig. 2). Additionally, PCOs are genetically highly consistent with original cancer and remain stable over time. In 2016, Jarno et al. [21] first cultured organoids derived from human metastatic prostate cancer biopsies and described a specific culture protocol. Their culture protocol allows the growth of both the luminal and basal prostatic epithelial lineages and the growth of advanced prostate cancers. Organoids established using this protocol can be used to study many different aspects of prostate cancer, including homeostasis, cancerogenesis and drug discovery. In 2018, Park et al. [41] generated neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) organoids from benign prostate epithelial cells via the lentiviral transfection of oncogenes, providing important insights into the drivers of prostate cancer progression. Furthermore, Servant et al. [42]. developed a biobank consisting of PCOs derived from 81 patients with primary and metastatic prostate cancer. They found radical prostatectomy (RP)-derived organoids had higher efficiency and maintained longer term than transurethral    resection of prostate (TURP)-derived organoids.

Below is a concise, evidence-based overview of “cell line organoids” (organoid systems initiated with or modeled after established immortalized or transformed cell lines), how they are made, their advantages and limits, and key application domains.

What “cell line organoids” are and where they fit
- Organoids are 3D cultures that better preserve tissue architecture, cell-type composition, and (epi)genetic heterogeneity than traditional 2D immortalized cell lines, yet they are more complex than simple spheroids and still face standardization and throughput challenges relative to cell lines and high-throughput cell-line banks <cite id="bf13eb6b-0">Organoids retain the 3D structure of the original tissues, faithfully summarizing the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity of the original tissue</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Two-dimensional immortalized cell lines are generally considered non-physiological due to lack of tissue architecture and genetic drift across batches</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-3">Organoids can reproduce tissue layers and structures and can be frozen like cell lines, offering more realistic in vitro modeling than cell lines</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-4">Organoid technology accelerates disease modeling but requires standardization and scaled production; throughput is limited by ECM gels and automation</cite>. 
- In the central nervous system, “spheroids” can be formed from primary cells or immortalized lines, whereas “organoids” are typically stem-cell–derived 3D self-organizing structures; both leverage 3D cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions to approximate in vivo organization for drug screening, developmental biology, and pathology <cite id="7e8f2221-0">Spheroids are 3D aggregates from primary cells or immortalized cell lines; organoids are stem-cell–derived 3D aggregates that self-organize to recapitulate tissue characteristics</cite>. 
- Conceptually, organoids are positioned between conventional cell lines and patient-derived xenografts (PDX), aiming to combine genetic fidelity and physiological complexity with practicality for screening and precision medicine <cite id="bf13eb6b-0">Organoids fill the gap between cell line and PDX, support existing model systems, and extend research to the human context</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Organoids are derived from small patient samples with high efficiency and better recapitulate architecture and functions than cell lines</cite>.

How cell line–based organoids are generated
- Epithelial/intestinal organoids (gut and pancreas): Canonical protocols culture Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells in Matrigel with niche factors (WNT agonists via R-spondin, EGF, Noggin) to sustain self-renewal and crypt–villus morphogenesis; similar strategies adapted human intestinal and colon organoids and informed later organoid engineering <cite id="335bd1d1-0">Single Lgr5+ stem cells embedded in Matrigel with WNT, Noggin, R-spondin and EGF form continuously expanding crypt–villus organoids with near-physiological epithelium</cite><cite id="335bd1d1-2">Human intestinal organoids were adapted from the 2009 system; organoids from colon and stomach with Lgr5+ stem cells followed</cite><cite id="335bd1d1-3">Intestinal organoids derived from PSCs can be matured in Matrigel into polarized epithelium with villus-like and crypt-like structures</cite><cite id="335bd1d1-4">A cytokine- and Matrigel-free protocol was developed to enable higher-throughput intestinal organoid screening</cite>. 
- Patient-derived and hybrid models: When primary tissue is scarce or difficult, organoids can be initiated from tumor biopsies and then expanded or complemented with PDX to generate organoid biobanks; PDX-organoid hybrids reduce time/cost while providing sufficient material for downstream organoid establishment <cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Organoids can be derived from small patient samples with high efficiency and are suitable for drug response prediction</cite><cite id="ae19e242-4">A PDX-organoid model takes less time and cost than PDX and provides adequate tissue for organoid establishment</cite>. 
- Prostate cancer organoids from established cell lines: To address representativeness limits of traditional PCa cell lines, organoids were directly generated “from currently available cell lines,” reproducing recurrent copy-number and mutation profiles (e.g., PTEN loss, CHD1, SPOP, FOXA1), with high intra-organoid genetic consistency and stability over time; subsequent protocols for biopsy-derived PCa organoids established long-term cultures spanning luminal/basal lineages and aggressive disease states <cite id="ae19e242-0">Gao et al. developed seven metastatic PCa organoids using available cell lines that reproduced PTEN loss and CHD1, SPOP, and FOXA1 alterations and remained genetically stable; Jarno et al. established a biopsy-derived culture protocol supporting luminal/basal lineages and advanced cancers</cite><cite id="ae19e242-1">PCa organoids from cell lines retained mutation profiles including PTEN loss and CHD1, SPOP, FOXA1 mutations and showed genetic stability over time</cite>. 
- Practical prostate organoid culture from tissue and lines: Organoids can be initiated from diverse PCa specimens and grown in Matrigel with optimized media; growth rates are slower than many other cancers; protocols address overgrowth by benign epithelium and basal cells, yielding luminal phenotypes; additionally, PCa cell lines (e.g., LNCaP, C4-2B) and single luminal progenitors can generate prostate organoids with androgen-dependent or non-androgen-dependent characteristics <cite id="ae19e242-3">Prostate organoids embedded in Matrigel using optimized media maintain acinar/solid structures and show slower growth than other tumor organoids; protocols reduce basal cell presence to yield luminal phenotypes</cite><cite id="ae19e242-0">LNCaP and C4-2B can produce prostate organoids with androgen-dependent and non-androgen-dependent models, respectively</cite><cite id="ae19e242-4">Organoids from mouse and human tissues recapitulate AR signaling, basal/luminal markers, and fusion/alteration phenotypes; LNCaP, C4-2B, and single luminal progenitors can produce PCa organoids</cite>. 
- Neural organoids and spheroids from immortalized lines: Brain organoids/“mini-brains” are commonly derived from pluripotent stem cells via self-organization protocols (e.g., SFEBq, dual-SMAD inhibition spheroid culture) to recapitulate regional development and enable disease modeling; in parallel, 3D brain spheroids routinely use primary cells or immortalized lines as the starting material, and organoids can be scaled with bioreactors and vascularization strategies to mitigate diffusion limits <cite id="7e8f2221-2">Neural organoids generated from pluripotent stem cells via SFEBq or neural spheroid protocols differentiate into region-specific 3D neural tissues</cite><cite id="7e8f2221-0">Spheroids are 3D aggregates from primary cells or immortalized lines, whereas organoids self-organize from stem cells to recapitulate tissue characteristics</cite><cite id="7e8f2221-3">Brain organoids derived from iPSCs are cultured in Matrigel droplets, often in bioreactors; vascularization strategies with vascular spheroids or ETV2 overexpression address diffusion limits</cite>.

Advantages and key applications of cell line–based organoids
- Genetic tractability and fidelity: Prostate cancer organoids derived from established cell lines closely reproduce hallmark alterations (e.g., PTEN loss, ERG–TMPRSS2 fusions, SPOP/FOXA1), offering models where genotype-to-phenotype relationships can be interrogated and tracked over time <cite id="ae19e242-0">Cell line–derived PCa organoids reproduced recurrent alterations (PTEN loss, CHD1, SPOP, FOXA1) and remained genetically stable</cite>. 
- Disease modeling and drug discovery: Organoids support precision oncology by retaining tumor heterogeneity and drug response features; prostate organoid biobanks have been established to probe oncogenic pathways (e.g., SPOP mutation effects on AR binding) and to test therapeutics in patient-specific matrices <cite id="ae19e242-2">Prostate organoids retained TME complexity and AR-related molecular programs; SPOP mutations altered AR binding patterns mirroring primary tumors</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Organoids better recapitulate architecture and functions for disease modeling and drug response prediction</cite>. 
- Virus and infection modeling: Organoids mimic organ-level physiology better than 2D lines, enabling realistic infection and antiviral screening while remaining amenable to genetic manipulation; however, cost and scalability constraints still limit full replacement of cell-line and animal models <cite id="bf13eb6b-3">Organoids can reproduce tissue layers and structures, can be frozen like cell lines, and better simulate in vivo phenomena for complex disease modeling</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-4">Organoid technology reduces animal use but needs standardization and scaled production; current culture costs and handling limit large-scale replacement</cite>. 
- Neurodevelopmental and neurological disease: Neural organoids capture early cortical development gene expression and cytoarchitecture, enabling mechanistic studies and drug testing; spheroids initiated from immortalized lines provide a practical entry point when primary tissue is limited <cite id="7e8f2221-3">Brain organoids recapitulate fetal neocortex gene programs and support diverse readouts for drug screening and mechanistic studies</cite><cite id="7e8f2221-0">Spheroids from immortalized lines are widely used as precursors to organoid systems</cite>. 
- High-throughput and engineering: For epithelial organoids, medium and matrix optimizations (e.g., cytokine-free, low-Matrigel conditions) enable compatibility with automated screening and microfluidic platforms, expanding throughput while retaining core biological features <cite id="335bd1d1-4">A cytokine- and Matrigel-free protocol was developed to support high-throughput screening of intestinal organoids</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Some groups culture organoids in lower ECM to adapt to high-throughput screening using microfluidic systems</cite>.

Limitations, caveats, and engineering strategies
- Representativeness and drift: Immortalized 2D lines often diverge from tissue-of-origin genotype and phenotypes and exhibit non-physiological architecture; cell line–derived organoids can close this gap but may still carry founder-effect biases and genetic drift over time <cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Cell lines established decades ago no longer faithfully represent their tissue of origin and show genetic drift across batches</cite><cite id="ae19e242-0">Prostate cell lines fail to reflect recurrent lesions like TMPRSS2-ERG fusions and CHD1 deletions, SPOP and FOXA1 mutations</cite>. 
- Organoid fidelity vs. throughput: While organoids better model physiology, ECM gels and complex architectures challenge automation and high-throughput screening; strategies include lower ECM density, microfluidics, and standardization of culture conditions to balance fidelity and scalability <cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Organoids’ ECM gels limit automated high-throughput handling; low-gel or gel-free conditions and microfluidics are being explored</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-4">Standardization and scalable production are necessary for broader applications</cite>. 
- Protocol and lineage control: Prostate organoid protocols must manage overgrowth by benign epithelium and basal cell populations to maintain luminal phenotypes; growth kinetics are slower in some cancers, requiring patient stratification and careful readouts <cite id="ae19e242-3">PC organoids initially face overgrowth by benign epithelium and basal cells; optimized cultures yield luminal phenotypes and show slower growth rates</cite>. 
- Genetic and phenotypic engineering: Combining organoid culture with CRISPR enables precise mutation modeling (e.g., AR pathway variants, SPOP alterations) and co-culture/biobank strategies to expand genetic diversity and functional readouts <cite id="bf13eb6b-0">CRISPR–Cas9 with organoids provides opportunities to study tumor gene mutations</cite><cite id="ae19e242-2">SPOP mutation impacts AR binding patterns in organoids, paralleling native tumors</cite>.

Practical takeaways and when to use cell line–based organoids
- Use established cell-line organoids when primary tissue is limited or when you need genetically defined, tractable models with known driver landscapes (e.g., CRPC/LNCaP/C4-2B prostate organoids) to study oncogenic programs, drug response, and pathway perturbations <cite id="ae19e242-0">Cell line–derived PCa organoids reproduce recurrent alterations and offer genetically stable systems for modeling</cite><cite id="ae19e242-4">LNCaP and C4-2B produce organoids with distinct androgen dependence, useful for precision models</cite>. 
- For infectious disease and multi-cellular organ-level mechanisms, spheroids initiated from immortalized lines and organoids from PSCs provide practical platforms before scaling up to patient-derived organoids; integrate bioreactor culture and vascularization to improve viability and maturation <cite id="7e8f2221-0">Spheroids from immortalized lines are established practices for brain models</cite><cite id="7e8f2221-3">Bioreactor culture and vascularization strategies (e.g., co-assembly with vascular spheroids or ETV2 activation) mitigate diffusion limits</cite>. 
- To maximize relevance and reproducibility, pair cell line–derived organoids with rigorous barcoding/longitudinal genotyping, matrix/medium standardization, and cross-checks against patient-derived organoids or PDX; where feasible, move to cytokine/matrix-optimized or microfluidic formats for higher-throughput screening <cite id="bf13eb6b-2">Longitudinal culture standardization and low-gel/microfluidic adaptations improve throughput and comparability</cite><cite id="bf13eb6b-0">Organoid banks and CRISPR-based perturbations can build comprehensive experimental platforms</cite>.

- Organ specificity: While strong evidence exists for gut and prostate systems, direct protocols for liver organoids initiated from widely used hepatocellular carcinoma lines (e.g., HepG2, Huh7) were not captured in the retrieved snippets; similar gaps exist for definitive “TOP-NHDF feeder” protocols for human gut organoids beyond foundational niche-factor culture. Title: Genome engineering of stem cell organoids for disease modeling
Snippet: The development of the intestinal organoid culture system in 2009 was a major technological advance in this field (Sato et al., 2009). In this study, single Lgr5 + stem cells were isolated from mouse intestinal epithelium and cultured in a simple 3D culture system in which Matrigel was used as extra cellular matrix. A few key growth factors, such as WNT, Noggin, R-spondin and EGF, were supplemented mostly to maintain stem cell populations. Remarkably, these stem cells were found later to be able to form continuously expanding crypt-villus organoids that present near-physiological epithelium architecture reminiscent of normal gut. A similar culture system was subsequently adapted for generation of human intestinal organoids (Dekkers et al., 2013). Moreover, Lgr5 + stem cells derived from other organs were also found later to be able to self-organize to form different organoids, including stomach, colon and liver (Barker et al., 2010;Huch et al., 2013a, b;Sato et al., 2011;Stange et al., 2013).

Snippet: The system was subsequently adapted for not only generating human intestinal organoids, but also organoids derived from other organs, particularly from colon and stomach having Lgr5+ stem cells [230][231][232][233]. This first report of establishing 3D organoid culture derived from a single ASC was followed by many subsequent organoid works in mesendoderm (e.g., stomach, liver, pancreas, lung, and kidney) and neuroectoderm (brain and retina) systems [230][231][232][233][234]. 

Although the earliest 3D epithelial organoid models were first described over 40 years ago, their limited in vitro viability prevented them from being used in translational medicine. These drawbacks are now largely excluded along with advances and extensive research on multipotent stem and progenitor cell isolation. In 2009, Sato et al. [230] were able to produce indefinite expansion of self-renewing intestinal organoids. The proposed method conducted intestinal crypts and FAC sorted Lgr5+ intestinal epithelium cells em-bedded in a 3D matrix called Matrigel [230]. After optimizing this method, we are now able to produce organoids from human colon and colorectal adenoma tissue noting that the Clevers group are the ones who derived epithelial organoid models from human colorectal cancers [230,235,236]. The characteristics of these 3D epithelial organoids are multipotent cellular differentiation, biologically relevant cellular signaling, and a complex intercellular communication and organization network. 

In a culture medium supplemented with EGF, noggin and the Wnt agonist R-spondin (RSPO), intestinal organoids were able to be established. The protocol was developed by embedding the intestinal stem cells in a 3D Matrigel. The protocol followed is now required during in vitro tissue development and in adult homeostasis and repair. By merging the knowledge on stem cell populations and utilizing information from the intestinal stem-cell niche requirements, intestinal organoids from either postnatal or adult intestinal epithelium [237] or from a single adult intestinal stem cell [230] were established.

Title: Progress, prospects, and limitations of organoid technology
Snippet: In 2009, Sato et al. [6] first established intestinal organoids derived from leucine-rich repeat-containing G protein-coupled receptor 5 (Lgr5)+ stem cells using a Matrigel 3D culture system. These organoids form crypt-villus structures with cellular heterogeneity to mimic the physiology and organization of the actual intestine. When transplanted into mice, intestinal organoids showed long-term survival, and their regenerative ability was also confirmed [32]. Hindgut spheroids were cultured from human PSCs in Matrigel to promote the maturation of intestinal organoids. Although intestinal organoids are derived from PSCs, gastric and lingual organoids-derived from parts of the digestive tract-are generated from adult pyloric stem cells and adult tongue epithelium, respectively [33]. Organoid technology can be used as a powerful tool to study gastrointestinal diseases, intestine-microbe interactions, and colorectal cancer.

Snippet: However, due to the differences in anatomy, biochemistry, and microorganisms in the gastrointestinal tissues of species, and to avoid the cost and efforts required for animal studies, a highly predictive in vitro assessment system is required. 

Recently, fabrication methods for human intestinal organoids from intestinal epithelial stem cells (Sato et al., 2009) or PSCs (Spence et al., 2011;Takahashi et al., 2018) have been reported. In 2009, Sato et al. showed for the first time that intestinal epithelial tissue organoids could be constructed from Lgr5-positive stem cells isolated from crypt regions in the small intestine (Sato et al., 2009). Title: Urological cancer organoids, patients' avatars for precision medicine: past, present and future
Snippet: Over the past century, only seven prostate cancer cell lines have been established, six from biopsy samples of patients with metastatic prostate cancer and one from circulating tumour cells (CTCs). Although cell lines are easy to culture, they fail to reflect common recurrent genetic lesions in prostate cancer such as TMPRSS2-ERG and CHD1 deletions, SPOP and FOXA1 mutations [36]. 

To fix this research gap, Schroe et al. [37] firstly reported  [38]. However, prostate cancer xenotransplantation has a low success rate ranging from 20 to 75% in subcutaneous models [39]. Nonetheless, the emergence of organoids is a promising solution. 

In 2014, Gao et al. [40] first developed seven metastatic prostate cancer organoids (PCOs) using currently available cell lines and demonstrated that PCOs could reproduce characteristic copy number and mutation profiles commonly found in prostate cancer, including the loss of PTEN and CHD1, SPOP and FOXA1 mutations (Fig. 2). Additionally, PCOs are genetically highly consistent with original cancer and remain stable over time. In 2016, Jarno et al. [21] first cultured organoids derived from human metastatic prostate cancer biopsies and described a specific culture protocol. Their culture protocol allows the growth of both the luminal and basal prostatic epithelial lineages and the growth of advanced prostate cancers. Organoids established using this protocol can be used to study many different aspects of prostate cancer, including homeostasis, cancerogenesis and drug discovery. In 2018, Park et al. [41] generated neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) organoids from benign prostate epithelial cells via the lentiviral transfection of oncogenes, providing important insights into the drivers of prostate cancer progression. Furthermore, Servant et al. [42]. developed a biobank consisting of PCOs derived from 81 patients with primary and metastatic prostate cancer. They found radical prostatectomy (RP)-derived organoids had higher efficiency and maintained longer term than transurethral    resection of prostate (TURP)-derived organoids.

Among these organoid lines, eight (LPC-1 through LPC-8) were established from LPC tissues, while the ninth (CRPC) was derived from CRPC tissue localized to the prostate gland (Fig 1B ). 

PC organoids exhibited morphological features similar to those of patient tumor tissues (Fig 1B). To further characterize the PC organoid cultures, immunohistochemical analyses were performed using the luminal cell marker keratin 8 (KRT8) and the basal cell marker keratin 5 (KRT5). In comparison, the established PC organoids exhibited a luminal phenotype with the absence of basal cells (Fig 1B ).

Snippet: The specimen for organoid culture can be derived from any stage of tumor development and only a small piece of tissue or few cells are required to culture in vitro (47). Thus, different phenotypes of PCa organoids have been successfully cultivated. Karthaus et al. (28) used mouse prostate epithelial cells and human prostate specimens to cultivate normal prostate organoids composed of fully differentiated CK5 + basal cells and CK8 + luminal cells. (49) successfully cultured four neuroendocrine-like PCa organoids from metastatic biopsy specimens, including simple small cell carcinoma and high-grade carcinoma with extensive neuroendocrine differentiation. The specimen for organoid culture can be derived from any stage of tumor development and only a small piece of tissue or few cells are required to culture in vitro (47). Thus, different phenotypes of PCa organoids have been successfully cultivated. Karthaus et al. (28) used mouse prostate epithelial cells and human prostate specimens to cultivate normal prostate organoids composed of fully differentiated CK5 + basal cells and CK8 + luminal cells. It was found that such organoids retained the expression of AR signaling factors, prostate-specific transcription factor Nkx3.1, basal cell markers p63 and CK5, and luminal cell marker CK8. At the same time, the original tissues of mouse with PTEN knockout and TMPRSS2-ERG fusion gene were cultured in organoids, and the phenotypes were consistent. Additionally, Gao et al. (17) successfully cultivated seven metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC)-type organoids from biopsy tissue   (48). Currently, there are only a few effective models for the study of neuroendocrine tumors. Puca et al. (49) successfully cultured four neuroendocrine-like PCa organoids from metastatic biopsy specimens, including simple small cell carcinoma and high-grade carcinoma with extensive neuroendocrine differentiation. They reported that the organoid model is a good tool for further understanding the characteristics of NEPC. Currently, androgen-sensitive and hormone-insensitive CRPC organoid models have been established, and CRPC transformation models have also been reported. Additionally, PCa cell lines LNCaP, C4-2B, and single luminal epithelial progenitors can also produce PCa organoids (29,50). LNCaP produces androgen-dependent models while C4-2B produces a non-androgen-dependent model, each representing different clinical characteristics. 

Recently, a novel in vitro modeling system combining the advantages of organoids and PDX has been reported (51). The PDX-organoid model takes less time and costs less than the PDX model and provides an adequate source of tissue for the establishment of organoid models.

documents.title: Urological cancer organoids, patients' avatars for precision medicine: past, present and future
documents.snippet:
Over the past century, only seven prostate cancer cell lines have been established, six from biopsy samples of patients with metastatic prostate cancer and one from circulating tumour cells (CTCs). Although cell lines are easy to culture, they fail to reflect common recurrent genetic lesions in prostate cancer such as TMPRSS2-ERG and CHD1 deletions, SPOP and FOXA1 mutations [36]. 

To fix this research gap, Schroe et al. [37] firstly reported  [38]. However, prostate cancer xenotransplantation has a low success rate ranging from 20 to 75% in subcutaneous models [39]. Nonetheless, the emergence of organoids is a promising solution. 

In 2014, Gao et al. [40] first developed seven metastatic prostate cancer organoids (PCOs) using currently available cell lines and demonstrated that PCOs could reproduce characteristic copy number and mutation profiles commonly found in prostate cancer, including the loss of PTEN and CHD1, SPOP and FOXA1 mutations (Fig. 2). Additionally, PCOs are genetically highly consistent with original cancer and remain stable over time. In 2016, Jarno et al. [21] first cultured organoids derived from human metastatic prostate cancer biopsies and described a specific culture protocol. Their culture protocol allows the growth of both the luminal and basal prostatic epithelial lineages and the growth of advanced prostate cancers. Organoids established using this protocol can be used to study many different aspects of prostate cancer, including homeostasis, cancerogenesis and drug discovery. In 2018, Park et al. [41] generated neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) organoids from benign prostate epithelial cells via the lentiviral transfection of oncogenes, providing important insights into the drivers of prostate cancer progression. Furthermore, Servant et al. [42]. developed a biobank consisting of PCOs derived from 81 patients with primary and metastatic prostate cancer. They found radical prostatectomy (RP)-derived organoids had higher efficiency and maintained longer term than transurethral    resection of prostate (TURP)-derived organoids.

documents.title: Tumor organoids: applications in cancer modeling and potentials in precision medicine
documents.snippet: Prostate cancer (PC) represents one of the most common cancer types in males and has an increasing incidence worldwide; it also ranks among the highest level of cancer-related mortality in males [122]. Many studies have employed organoids to investigate tumor biology and promote tumor translational medicine [19,[123][124][125][126][127][128][129][130][131][132][133]. Heninger E and colleagues established PDOs from locally advanced PC [134]. According to orthogonal analyses, these organoids retained the complexity of the TME observed in multifocal PC [134]. According to an orthogonal flow cytometry analysis, PC organoids retained a distinct subpopulation of epithelial cells that conserved the expression of AR-related molecules [134]. Based on genetically normal mouse prostate organoids, SPOP mutation contributes to accessibility and AR binding patterns that are similar to those of native primary tumors [135].

Among these organoid lines, eight (LPC-1 through LPC-8) were established from LPC tissues, while the ninth (CRPC) was derived from CRPC tissue localized to the prostate gland (Fig 1B ). 

PC organoids exhibited morphological features similar to those of patient tumor tissues (Fig 1B). PC organoids maintained their acinar or solid structures and displayed a triad of morphologies-solid, cystic, and poly-cystic (Fig 1B -D)-within a one-week span post embedding. While tumor organoids derived from LPC showed various morphologies, those derived from CRPC tumor tissue primarily formed solid structures (Fig 1D). Given that PC typically exhibits slower growth compared to other cancer types, the individual PC organoid lines also displayed a relatively slower growth rate than other types of tumor organoids (Fig 1E) [27][28][29][30][31][32][33]. On average, it took approximately 20 days for these tumor organoids to reach a diameter of 100-200 μm (Fig 1E). Based on the Gleason score, T stage, and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level, we observed no discernible bias in organoid establishment when comparing the stratification of all tumor tissue samples with that of established patient-derived PC organoid lines (Fig 1F). 

To further characterize the PC organoid cultures, immunohistochemical analyses were performed using the luminal cell marker keratin 8 (KRT8) and the basal cell marker keratin 5 (KRT5). During the process of tumor organoid establishment from primary PC specimens, previous studies encountered challenges related to the overgrowth of benign epithelial cells as well as the presence of significant basal cells [13,34]. In comparison, the established PC organoids exhibited a luminal phenotype with the absence of basal cells (Fig 1B ).

Title: The neurovascular unit in leukodystrophies: towards solving the puzzle
Snippet: Using hiPSCs, it is possible to engineer several different strategies to explore brain homeostasis and disorders. A major breakthrough is the technique to culture cerebral organoids [166,167]. The definition of organoid is still quite controversial, and some researchers struggle with the line between a spheroid and an organoid. Even so, it is generally agreed that, while spheroids are 3D cultures consisting of cell aggregates established from primary cells or immortalized cell lines, organoids are stem cellderived 3D cell aggregates that self-organize to recapitulate some of the endogenous tissue characteristics [168]. These 3D structures constitute a physiologically relevant tool for drug screening, developmental biology, and pathology, by allowing for cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions in an in vivo-like organization, in contrast to 2D systems [169,170].

Title: Experimental Models for Testing the Efficacy of Pharmacological Treatments for Neonatal Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy
Snippet: An influential class of supracellular models is represented by pluripotent stem cells, which show a remarkable ability to self-organize and differentiate in vitro in three-dimensional aggregates, known as organoids or organ spheroids, recapitulating aspects of human brain development and function. Region-specific 3D brain cultures can be assembled to model complex cell-cell interactions and to generate circuits in human brain assembloids. Brain region-specific spheroids can undergo different maturation stages and can mimic immature brain conditions and maturation [21]. Human 3D brain-region-specific organoids can be utilized to study the effect of hypoxic insults utilizing a variety of read outs, including live-cell imaging, calcium dynamics, electrophysiology, cell purification, single-cell transcriptomics, and immunohistochemistry studies. Despite the challenges posed by the heterogeneous nature of brain organoids generated from pluripotent stem cells, such a human cell-based 3D model is potentially amenable to drug screening and to mechanistically studying neuroprotective therapies. [22].
